title: Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Gradients Unlock Topological Dimensional Reduction in Magnetic Hopfions
authors: Kui Yuan, Hailong Shen, Jiawei Dong, Xin Zhang, Longqing Chen, Yihan Wang, Bo Liu, Qing Zhang, Zhengshang Wang, Wenbin Qiu, Xiaoyi Wang, Bing Han, Yang Qiu, Kun Zhang, Xudong Cui
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetic solitons retain topological protection only while their spin field remains continuous. Here we show that chemical inhomogeneity can break this protection in a controlled way, converting a hopfion-like toroidal texture into an effectively two-dimensional skyrmion string. Tilt-dependent Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and micromagnetic simulations of pristine, uniformly Y-doped, and nonuniformly Y-doped disordered TiO2 nanoparticles embedded in a FeCrNiMn host reveal two regimes. Uniform Y doping enriches Ti3+/oxygen-vacancy localization centers and stabilizes closed rings with Hopf invariant QH approximately 1. Nonuniform Y doping forms a Ti4+-rich, vacancy-depleted boundary that creates a sharp q=D/(2A) gradient and a weak-moment leakage channel. This coupled mismatch torque and continuity leakage split the ring, leaving a skyrmion-string remnant and a field-sensitive helicity texture.
summary: This work demonstrates that chemical disorder (Y doping) can be used as a tool to manipulate the topology of magnetic structures in $	ext{TiO}_2$ nanoparticles. By creating sharp gradients, the system forces a transition from stable 3D Hopfions into lower-dimensional skyrmion strings. This provides a mechanism for controlling topological states using material engineering.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlled chemical inhomogeneity can break the topological protection of three-dimensional magnetic solitons (Hopfions), causing them to reduce dimensionality into effectively two-dimensional skyrmion strings.
main_result: Nonuniform Y doping creates a sharp gradient in the effective Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction parameter ($q$), leading to the asymmetric splitting of the toroidal texture into stable skyrmion string remnants and topologically trivial branches.
method: The research combines experimental characterization using Tilt-dependent Lorentz TEM and EELS with theoretical modeling via micromagnetic simulations.
model_or_system: The system involves disordered TiO2 nanoparticles embedded in an FeCrNiMn host, where magnetism arises from localized Ti3+/oxygen-vacancy centers. The model analyzes the competition between interfacial mismatch energy (due to gradients) and elastic curvature energy.
key_observables: Topological invariants like Hopf invariant ($	ext{QH}$) and Skyrmion charge ($Q$); magnetic domain maps; electronic states ($	ext{Ti}^{3+}$ vs $	ext{Ti}^{4+}$).
important_parameters: The ratio $q=D/(2A)$; the degree of Y doping (uniform vs. nonuniform); local spin continuity.
main_assumptions: Effective micromagnetic parameters are used for defect-induced textures; simulations introduce confinement barriers to suppress artificial topological leakage.
figures_summary: Figures compare LTEM images and spectra across pristine, uniformly doped, and nonuniformly doped samples, illustrating the transition from stable rings to bifurcated skyrmion strings under varying magnetic fields.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the baseline (pristine/uniform doping) showing robust 3D textures, then introducing the gradient via nonuniform doping, which is shown experimentally and simulated to cause the topological splitting mechanism.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the concept of controlled defect engineering to induce a specific symmetry breaking or dimensionality reduction in a topologically protected state shares conceptual parallels with engineered quantum interfaces or boundary effects studied in AMO physics.
